issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: The negative appraisal items 'others can see what happened to me' and 'ashamed of what happened to my body' imply a trauma with visible bodily violation or injury, most classically interpersonal/sexual trauma, and are hard to reconcile with a generic man-made disaster trauma in the absence of any corroborating memory or trigger content about bodily injury or disfigurement.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Being Touched' is specifically linked to bodily violation/contact-based trauma and fits poorly with the rest of the profile for man-made disaster. The threat items center on environmental danger and escape planning, creating a cross-node mismatch with this touch-avoidance strategy.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: These items imply a trauma with prominent bodily violation or physical injury consequences. For a man-made disaster trauma, this specific body-focused pattern is not impossible, but in the absence of any supporting memory or trigger content and alongside the other items emphasizing generalized danger, it stands out as a hard-to-explain shift toward an assault/injury formulation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
issues.explanation: Within the current profile, avoidance of touch and bodily stress appears organized around bodily harm/shame, but the threat items are about environmental danger, escape planning, and unfamiliar places. That makes the strategy set only partially connected to the expressed threat/appraisal pattern.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: The profile is otherwise centered on persistent danger, vigilance, scanning, escape planning, and avoidance of unfamiliar places, which coheres with threat-focused beliefs after a man-made disaster. 'Failed Role' introduces a distinct self-evaluative theme that is not supported by the rest of the selected items and is hard to reconcile with this otherwise purely danger/safety formulation. Given the active formulation emphasizes Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies and Maladaptive Strategies → Threat, a danger-based appraisal would better fit the linked hypervigilance and checking strategies than a role-failure appraisal.

vignette: Meera, a 32-year-old South Asian woman and city council member, has been experiencing significant psychological distress following a man-made disaster that occurred in her community. The event was traumatic not only because of the immediate danger but also due to the subsequent chaos and unpredictability it unleashed on her daily life. Since the incident, Meera’s world feels fundamentally different. She now believes the world is inherently dangerous, a notion deeply rooted in her experience during the disaster when she felt utterly vulnerable and at risk. This belief has led her to adopt several maladaptive strategies as coping mechanisms. For instance, she avoids any situations that put her body under stress, such as public gatherings or physical exertion, fearing it might make her more susceptible to harm. One of Meera’s primary concerns is staying vigilant for any signs of danger. She constantly scans her environment, especially in unfamiliar places, where she feels unable to assess the level of threat accurately. This hypervigilance has become a part of her daily routine, even extending into her work as a city council member. During meetings or public events, she finds herself constantly scanning for escape routes and watching people closely, looking for any signs that might indicate potential threats. The disaster has made Meera particularly anxious about the night-time, when darkness amplifies her sense of vulnerability. She feels much safer during daylight hours but is haunted by a perpetual fear that something could happen at any moment. This heightened state of vigilance and constant scanning for danger have become all-consuming, leading to further negative appraisals. She now believes she must be on guard constantly because you never know what can happen next. These beliefs have influenced Meera’s behavior in numerous ways. For example, her decision to avoid unfamiliar places is driven by the fear that she cannot adequately assess their safety. This avoidance has affected her work as a city council member, limiting her ability to engage with diverse communities and attend important meetings held at new locations. Additionally, she always tries to identify escape routes before feeling comfortable anywhere, which often leads to feelings of disconnection from others who do not share this need for constant security. The interplay between Meera’s negative appraisals and maladaptive strategies has created a self-reinforcing cycle that makes her daily life increasingly restrictive. Her belief in the dangerous nature of the world drives her to avoid stress-inducing situations, which in turn reinforces her sense of threat and hypervigilance. This ongoing loop has left Meera feeling isolated and anxious. What finally prompted Meera to seek help was a series of missed meetings and public events due to her fear of unfamiliar places. She realized that her work as a city council member was suffering, and she felt unable to fulfill her duties effectively without these coping mechanisms. Despite the relief she finds in these strategies, what frightens her most is the realization that they are limiting her ability to engage with the community she serves. Meera hopes for a way to regain some sense of safety and control over her life without having to avoid so many aspects of daily living. She wants to be able to go about her work and personal activities without feeling constantly threatened, and is eager to find strategies that will help her manage her fear and hypervigilance more effectively. The experience has made Meera acutely aware of the unpredictability and danger she perceives in the world around her, but she is determined to break free from this cycle and reclaim a sense of normalcy.
